case_info.scenario: A previously healthy 25-year-old woman presented with headache, dysarthria, double vision, and dizziness for 1 week. She denied any history of fever, head trauma, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, or cough. She had traveled to northeastern Brazil 2 months before the onset of the neurological symptoms. On examination, she had a mild right-side hemiparesis with hyperreflexia and hemiataxia. She could walk unassisted but presented with a broad base. There were no meningeal signs. She did not present with hepatosplenomegaly of lymphadenopathy. Her cranial magnetic resonance imaging  showed a T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintense lesion with heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement in the pons (Figure). There were no signs of diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging or hemorrhages on susceptibility-weighted imaging. The laboratory test results showed a hemoglobin level of 15.3 g/dL (to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10.0), total leukocyte count of 10 390/uL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001), of which 1703 (16.4%) were eosinophils, and a platelet count of 284 000/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). The patient’s liver and kidney function test results were normal. Computed tomography of the chest revealed bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltrates. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed 640 cells, of which 57% were lymphocytes, 26% were eosinophils, and 13% were monocytes; protein levels were 70 mg/dL, and glucose levels were 46 mg/dL. Her blood cultures were found to be sterile.
case_info.caption: Sagittal gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and sagittal T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) (B) showing the extent of the lesion.
case_info.explanation: Although listeriosis is a major cause of rhombencephalitis, the CSF typically does not show eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, and the patient’s blood and CSF cultures were sterile. Beyond listeriosis, other infections (herpesvirus infections and tuberculosis) and autoimmune diseases (Behçet disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis, demyelinating diseases, and paraneoplastic syndromes) may cause rhombencephalitis.1The patient presented with a nodular lesion with an heterogenous, multinodular, contrast-enhancing pattern consistent with a granulomatous disease (eg, infection by mycobacteria, fungi, parasite, or even sarcoidosis).2,3 The differential diagnosis is narrowed largely by the CSF characteristics. Eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is defined as the presence of more than 10 eosinophils/mm3in CSF and/or eosinophils accounting for more than 10% of cerebrospinal leukocytes.4The most common cause of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is invasion of the central nervous system by helminthic parasites, such asAngiostrongylus cantonensis, Gnathostomaspecies, Schistosoma mansoni,andTaenia solium.5Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis may present eosinophilia and neuromyelitis-optica spectrum disorders may present some eosinophils in the CSF, but we would not expect sufficient eosinophils to fulfill the definition of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis in these diseases. With the history of recent travel to northeastern Brazil, an endemic region forS mansoni, we ordered immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin M antibody tests for this parasite in the patient’s CSF, of which results were positive. We also tested for antibodies in the blood using the enzyme-linked immunoassay  method, of which results were undetermined. Different from antibodies in the CSF, antibody detection in blood samples cannot distinguish between prior and active infection and have limited specificity for the diagnosis of neuroschistomiasis in endemic areas.6 Results for Kato-Katz testing forS mansonieggs were negative. However, this test has low sensitivity, especially when a single sample is used because egg burden in feces may be uneven and may lack sensitivity in the acute phase of infection because it may take up to 2 months for the adult worms to deposit the eggs in the bowel wall.7 We believe the present patient fulfills the diagnosis of neuroschistosomiasis according to criteria proposed by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention8: (1) typical syndrome as eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is suggestive of an infection caused by helminths, including schistosomiasis, (2) evidence of schistosomiasis demonstrated by the presence of positive immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G  antibodies forS mansoniin the CSF, and (3) a reasonable exclusion of the differential diagnosis. Neuroschistosomiasis can develop during any stage of the infection byS mansoni.However, an intense granulomatous response with clinically significant eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, eosinophilia, patchy pulmonary infiltrates, the presence of immunoglobulin M antibodies in the CSF, the absence of eggs in the Kato-Katz testing, and the presumed exposure are all suggestive of the acute phase of the infection that usually occurs 28 to 90 days after the infection and precedes oviposition.6 In Brazil, the most common presentation of neuroschistosomiasis is myeloradiculopathy owing to the parasite migration via the Batson venous plexus. However, case reports and a systematic review of 33 cases published from 1989 to 2019 of cerebral infection withS mansonishowed that brainstem lesions can also occur.9 There is a concern for initial worsening of neurologic symptoms with administration of anthelmintic therapy with praziquantel because the egg destruction may lead to further central nervous system inflammation. Although there is a lack of consensus on the optimal treatment of neuroschistosomiasis, many authors believe this complication can be prevented by corticosteroids, usually prednisone 1 to 2 mg/kg/d, started a few days before the initiation of praziquantel and continued for at least 2 months.10 Even with adequate therapy for neuroschistosomiasis, this patient presented with severe dysphagia and was submitted to orotracheal intubation. Unfortunately, she developed ventilator-associated complications and died.

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Clinical case]
A previously healthy 25-year-old woman presented with headache, dysarthria, double vision, and dizziness for 1 week. She denied any history of fever, head trauma, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, or cough. She had traveled to northeastern Brazil 2 months before the onset of the neurological symptoms. On examination, she had a mild right-side hemiparesis with hyperreflexia and hemiataxia. She could walk unassisted but presented with a broad base. There were no meningeal signs. She did not present with hepatosplenomegaly of lymphadenopathy. Her cranial magnetic resonance imaging  showed a T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintense lesion with heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement in the pons (Figure). There were no signs of diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging or hemorrhages on susceptibility-weighted imaging. The laboratory test results showed a hemoglobin level of 15.3 g/dL (to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10.0), total leukocyte count of 10 390/uL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001), of which 1703 (16.4%) were eosinophils, and a platelet count of 284 000/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). The patient’s liver and kidney function test results were normal. Computed tomography of the chest revealed bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltrates. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed 640 cells, of which 57% were lymphocytes, 26% were eosinophils, and 13% were monocytes; protein levels were 70 mg/dL, and glucose levels were 46 mg/dL. Her blood cultures were found to be sterile.

Neuroschistosomiasis typically presents with transverse myelitis or seizures, not a brainstem lesion, and is less associated with pulmonary findings. Let's confirm with serology or CSF PCR for Angiostrongylus before starting antiparasitics, as treatment differs.

case_info.explanation: Although listeriosis is a major cause of rhombencephalitis, the CSF typically does not show eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, and the patient’s blood and CSF cultures were sterile. Beyond listeriosis, other infections (herpesvirus infections and tuberculosis) and autoimmune diseases (Behçet disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis, demyelinating diseases, and paraneoplastic syndromes) may cause rhombencephalitis.1The patient presented with a nodular lesion with an heterogenous, multinodular, contrast-enhancing pattern consistent with a granulomatous disease (eg, infection by mycobacteria, fungi, parasite, or even sarcoidosis).2,3 The differential diagnosis is narrowed largely by the CSF characteristics. Eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is defined as the presence of more than 10 eosinophils/mm3in CSF and/or eosinophils accounting for more than 10% of cerebrospinal leukocytes.4The most common cause of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is invasion of the central nervous system by helminthic parasites, such asAngiostrongylus cantonensis, Gnathostomaspecies, Schistosoma mansoni,andTaenia solium.5Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis may present eosinophilia and neuromyelitis-optica spectrum disorders may present some eosinophils in the CSF, but we would not expect sufficient eosinophils to fulfill the definition of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis in these diseases. With the history of recent travel to northeastern Brazil, an endemic region forS mansoni, we ordered immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin M antibody tests for this parasite in the patient’s CSF, of which results were positive. We also tested for antibodies in the blood using the enzyme-linked immunoassay  method, of which results were undetermined. Different from antibodies in the CSF, antibody detection in blood samples cannot distinguish between prior and active infection and have limited specificity for the diagnosis of neuroschistomiasis in endemic areas.6 Results for Kato-Katz testing forS mansonieggs were negative. However, this test has low sensitivity, especially when a single sample is used because egg burden in feces may be uneven and may lack sensitivity in the acute phase of infection because it may take up to 2 months for the adult worms to deposit the eggs in the bowel wall.7 We believe the present patient fulfills the diagnosis of neuroschistosomiasis according to criteria proposed by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention8: (1) typical syndrome as eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is suggestive of an infection caused by helminths, including schistosomiasis, (2) evidence of schistosomiasis demonstrated by the presence of positive immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G  antibodies forS mansoniin the CSF, and (3) a reasonable exclusion of the differential diagnosis. Neuroschistosomiasis can develop during any stage of the infection byS mansoni.However, an intense granulomatous response with clinically significant eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, eosinophilia, patchy pulmonary infiltrates, the presence of immunoglobulin M antibodies in the CSF, the absence of eggs in the Kato-Katz testing, and the presumed exposure are all suggestive of the acute phase of the infection that usually occurs 28 to 90 days after the infection and precedes oviposition.6 In Brazil, the most common presentation of neuroschistosomiasis is myeloradiculopathy owing to the parasite migration via the Batson venous plexus. However, case reports and a systematic review of 33 cases published from 1989 to 2019 of cerebral infection withS mansonishowed that brainstem lesions can also occur.9 There is a concern for initial worsening of neurologic symptoms with administration of anthelmintic therapy with praziquantel because the egg destruction may lead to further central nervous system inflammation. Although there is a lack of consensus on the optimal treatment of neuroschistosomiasis, many authors believe this complication can be prevented by corticosteroids, usually prednisone 1 to 2 mg/kg/d, started a few days before the initiation of praziquantel and continued for at least 2 months.10 Even with adequate therapy for neuroschistosomiasis, this patient presented with severe dysphagia and was submitted to orotracheal intubation. Unfortunately, she developed ventilator-associated complications and died.

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a

  score low.)

  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

case_info.explanation: Although listeriosis is a major cause of rhombencephalitis, the CSF typically does not show eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, and the patient’s blood and CSF cultures were sterile. Beyond listeriosis, other infections (herpesvirus infections and tuberculosis) and autoimmune diseases (Behçet disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis, demyelinating diseases, and paraneoplastic syndromes) may cause rhombencephalitis.1The patient presented with a nodular lesion with an heterogenous, multinodular, contrast-enhancing pattern consistent with a granulomatous disease (eg, infection by mycobacteria, fungi, parasite, or even sarcoidosis).2,3 The differential diagnosis is narrowed largely by the CSF characteristics. Eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is defined as the presence of more than 10 eosinophils/mm3in CSF and/or eosinophils accounting for more than 10% of cerebrospinal leukocytes.4The most common cause of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is invasion of the central nervous system by helminthic parasites, such asAngiostrongylus cantonensis, Gnathostomaspecies, Schistosoma mansoni,andTaenia solium.5Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis may present eosinophilia and neuromyelitis-optica spectrum disorders may present some eosinophils in the CSF, but we would not expect sufficient eosinophils to fulfill the definition of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis in these diseases. With the history of recent travel to northeastern Brazil, an endemic region forS mansoni, we ordered immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin M antibody tests for this parasite in the patient’s CSF, of which results were positive. We also tested for antibodies in the blood using the enzyme-linked immunoassay  method, of which results were undetermined. Different from antibodies in the CSF, antibody detection in blood samples cannot distinguish between prior and active infection and have limited specificity for the diagnosis of neuroschistomiasis in endemic areas.6 Results for Kato-Katz testing forS mansonieggs were negative. However, this test has low sensitivity, especially when a single sample is used because egg burden in feces may be uneven and may lack sensitivity in the acute phase of infection because it may take up to 2 months for the adult worms to deposit the eggs in the bowel wall.7 We believe the present patient fulfills the diagnosis of neuroschistosomiasis according to criteria proposed by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention8: (1) typical syndrome as eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is suggestive of an infection caused by helminths, including schistosomiasis, (2) evidence of schistosomiasis demonstrated by the presence of positive immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G  antibodies forS mansoniin the CSF, and (3) a reasonable exclusion of the differential diagnosis. Neuroschistosomiasis can develop during any stage of the infection byS mansoni.However, an intense granulomatous response with clinically significant eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, eosinophilia, patchy pulmonary infiltrates, the presence of immunoglobulin M antibodies in the CSF, the absence of eggs in the Kato-Katz testing, and the presumed exposure are all suggestive of the acute phase of the infection that usually occurs 28 to 90 days after the infection and precedes oviposition.6 In Brazil, the most common presentation of neuroschistosomiasis is myeloradiculopathy owing to the parasite migration via the Batson venous plexus. However, case reports and a systematic review of 33 cases published from 1989 to 2019 of cerebral infection withS mansonishowed that brainstem lesions can also occur.9 There is a concern for initial worsening of neurologic symptoms with administration of anthelmintic therapy with praziquantel because the egg destruction may lead to further central nervous system inflammation. Although there is a lack of consensus on the optimal treatment of neuroschistosomiasis, many authors believe this complication can be prevented by corticosteroids, usually prednisone 1 to 2 mg/kg/d, started a few days before the initiation of praziquantel and continued for at least 2 months.10 Even with adequate therapy for neuroschistosomiasis, this patient presented with severe dysphagia and was submitted to orotracheal intubation. Unfortunately, she developed ventilator-associated complications and died.

case_info.explanation: Although listeriosis is a major cause of rhombencephalitis, the CSF typically does not show eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, and the patient’s blood and CSF cultures were sterile. Beyond listeriosis, other infections (herpesvirus infections and tuberculosis) and autoimmune diseases (Behçet disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis, demyelinating diseases, and paraneoplastic syndromes) may cause rhombencephalitis.1The patient presented with a nodular lesion with an heterogenous, multinodular, contrast-enhancing pattern consistent with a granulomatous disease (eg, infection by mycobacteria, fungi, parasite, or even sarcoidosis).2,3 The differential diagnosis is narrowed largely by the CSF characteristics. Eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is defined as the presence of more than 10 eosinophils/mm3in CSF and/or eosinophils accounting for more than 10% of cerebrospinal leukocytes.4The most common cause of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is invasion of the central nervous system by helminthic parasites, such asAngiostrongylus cantonensis, Gnathostomaspecies, Schistosoma mansoni,andTaenia solium.5Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis may present eosinophilia and neuromyelitis-optica spectrum disorders may present some eosinophils in the CSF, but we would not expect sufficient eosinophils to fulfill the definition of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis in these diseases. With the history of recent travel to northeastern Brazil, an endemic region forS mansoni, we ordered immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin M antibody tests for this parasite in the patient’s CSF, of which results were positive. case_info.explanation: Although listeriosis is a major cause of rhombencephalitis, the CSF typically does not show eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, and the patient’s blood and CSF cultures were sterile. Beyond listeriosis, other infections (herpesvirus infections and tuberculosis) and autoimmune diseases (Behçet disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis, demyelinating diseases, and paraneoplastic syndromes) may cause rhombencephalitis.1The patient presented with a nodular lesion with an heterogenous, multinodular, contrast-enhancing pattern consistent with a granulomatous disease (eg, infection by mycobacteria, fungi, parasite, or even sarcoidosis).2,3 The differential diagnosis is narrowed largely by the CSF characteristics. Eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is defined as the presence of more than 10 eosinophils/mm3in CSF and/or eosinophils accounting for more than 10% of cerebrospinal leukocytes.4The most common cause of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is invasion of the central nervous system by helminthic parasites, such asAngiostrongylus cantonensis, Gnathostomaspecies, Schistosoma mansoni,andTaenia solium.5Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis may present eosinophilia and neuromyelitis-optica spectrum disorders may present some eosinophils in the CSF, but we would not expect sufficient eosinophils to fulfill the definition of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis in these diseases. With the history of recent travel to northeastern Brazil, an endemic region forS mansoni, we ordered immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin M antibody tests for this parasite in the patient’s CSF, of which results were positive. We also tested for antibodies in the blood using the enzyme-linked immunoassay  method, of which results were undetermined. Different from antibodies in the CSF, antibody detection in blood samples cannot distinguish between prior and active infection and have limited specificity for the diagnosis of neuroschistomiasis in endemic areas.6 Results for Kato-Katz testing forS mansonieggs were negative. However, this test has low sensitivity, especially when a single sample is used because egg burden in feces may be uneven and may lack sensitivity in the acute phase of infection because it may take up to 2 months for the adult worms to deposit the eggs in the bowel wall.7 We believe the present patient fulfills the diagnosis of neuroschistosomiasis according to criteria proposed by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention8: (1) typical syndrome as eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is suggestive of an infection caused by helminths, including schistosomiasis, (2) evidence of schistosomiasis demonstrated by the presence of positive immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G  antibodies forS mansoniin the CSF, and (3) a reasonable exclusion of the differential diagnosis. Neuroschistosomiasis can develop during any stage of the infection byS mansoni.However, an intense granulomatous response with clinically significant eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, eosinophilia, patchy pulmonary infiltrates, the presence of immunoglobulin M antibodies in the CSF, the absence of eggs in the Kato-Katz testing, and the presumed exposure are all suggestive of the acute phase of the infection that usually occurs 28 to 90 days after the infection and precedes oviposition.6 In Brazil, the most common presentation of neuroschistosomiasis is myeloradiculopathy owing to the parasite migration via the Batson venous plexus. However, case reports and a systematic review of 33 cases published from 1989 to 2019 of cerebral infection withS mansonishowed that brainstem lesions can also occur.9 There is a concern for initial worsening of neurologic symptoms with administration of anthelmintic therapy with praziquantel because the egg destruction may lead to further central nervous system inflammation. Although there is a lack of consensus on the optimal treatment of neuroschistosomiasis, many authors believe this complication can be prevented by corticosteroids, usually prednisone 1 to 2 mg/kg/d, started a few days before the initiation of praziquantel and continued for at least 2 months.10 Even with adequate therapy for neuroschistosomiasis, this patient presented with severe dysphagia and was submitted to orotracheal intubation. Unfortunately, she developed ventilator-associated complications and died.

case_info.explanation: Although listeriosis is a major cause of rhombencephalitis, the CSF typically does not show eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, and the patient’s blood and CSF cultures were sterile. Beyond listeriosis, other infections (herpesvirus infections and tuberculosis) and autoimmune diseases (Behçet disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis, demyelinating diseases, and paraneoplastic syndromes) may cause rhombencephalitis.1The patient presented with a nodular lesion with an heterogenous, multinodular, contrast-enhancing pattern consistent with a granulomatous disease (eg, infection by mycobacteria, fungi, parasite, or even sarcoidosis).2,3 The differential diagnosis is narrowed largely by the CSF characteristics. Eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is defined as the presence of more than 10 eosinophils/mm3in CSF and/or eosinophils accounting for more than 10% of cerebrospinal leukocytes.4The most common cause of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is invasion of the central nervous system by helminthic parasites, such asAngiostrongylus cantonensis, Gnathostomaspecies, Schistosoma mansoni,andTaenia solium.5Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis may present eosinophilia and neuromyelitis-optica spectrum disorders may present some eosinophils in the CSF, but we would not expect sufficient eosinophils to fulfill the definition of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis in these diseases. With the history of recent travel to northeastern Brazil, an endemic region forS mansoni, we ordered immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin M antibody tests for this parasite in the patient’s CSF, of which results were positive. We also tested for antibodies in the blood using the enzyme-linked immunoassay  method, of which results were undetermined. Different from antibodies in the CSF, antibody detection in blood samples cannot distinguish between prior and active infection and have limited specificity for the diagnosis of neuroschistomiasis in endemic areas.6 Results for Kato-Katz testing forS mansonieggs were negative. However, this test has low sensitivity, especially when a single sample is used because egg burden in feces may be uneven and may lack sensitivity in the acute phase of infection because it may take up to 2 months for the adult worms to deposit the eggs in the bowel wall.7 We believe the present patient fulfills the diagnosis of neuroschistosomiasis according to criteria proposed by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention8: (1) typical syndrome as eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is suggestive of an infection caused by helminths, including schistosomiasis, (2) evidence of schistosomiasis demonstrated by the presence of positive immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G  antibodies forS mansoniin the CSF, and (3) a reasonable exclusion of the differential diagnosis. Neuroschistosomiasis can develop during any stage of the infection byS mansoni.However, an intense granulomatous response with clinically significant eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, eosinophilia, patchy pulmonary infiltrates, the presence of immunoglobulin M antibodies in the CSF, the absence of eggs in the Kato-Katz testing, and the presumed exposure are all suggestive of the acute phase of the infection that usually occurs 28 to 90 days after the infection and precedes oviposition.6 In Brazil, the most common presentation of neuroschistosomiasis is myeloradiculopathy owing to the parasite migration via the Batson venous plexus. However, case reports and a systematic review of 33 cases published from 1989 to 2019 of cerebral infection withS mansonishowed that brainstem lesions can also occur.9 There is a concern for initial worsening of neurologic symptoms with administration of anthelmintic therapy with praziquantel because the egg destruction may lead to further central nervous system inflammation. Although there is a lack of consensus on the optimal treatment of neuroschistosomiasis, many authors believe this complication can be prevented by corticosteroids, usually prednisone 1 to 2 mg/kg/d, started a few days before the initiation of praziquantel and continued for at least 2 months.10 Even with adequate therapy for neuroschistosomiasis, this patient presented with severe dysphagia and was submitted to orotracheal intubation. Unfortunately, she developed ventilator-associated complications and died.

case_info.scenario: A previously healthy 25-year-old woman presented with headache, dysarthria, double vision, and dizziness for 1 week. She denied any history of fever, head trauma, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, or cough. She had traveled to northeastern Brazil 2 months before the onset of the neurological symptoms. On examination, she had a mild right-side hemiparesis with hyperreflexia and hemiataxia. She could walk unassisted but presented with a broad base. There were no meningeal signs. She did not present with hepatosplenomegaly of lymphadenopathy. Her cranial magnetic resonance imaging  showed a T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintense lesion with heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement in the pons (Figure). There were no signs of diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging or hemorrhages on susceptibility-weighted imaging. The laboratory test results showed a hemoglobin level of 15.3 g/dL (to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10.0), total leukocyte count of 10 390/uL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001), of which 1703 (16.4%) were eosinophils, and a platelet count of 284 000/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). The patient’s liver and kidney function test results were normal. Computed tomography of the chest revealed bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltrates. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed 640 cells, of which 57% were lymphocytes, 26% were eosinophils, and 13% were monocytes; protein levels were 70 mg/dL, and glucose levels were 46 mg/dL. Her blood cultures were found to be sterile.

case_info.explanation: Although listeriosis is a major cause of rhombencephalitis, the CSF typically does not show eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, and the patient’s blood and CSF cultures were sterile. Beyond listeriosis, other infections (herpesvirus infections and tuberculosis) and autoimmune diseases (Behçet disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis, demyelinating diseases, and paraneoplastic syndromes) may cause rhombencephalitis.1The patient presented with a nodular lesion with an heterogenous, multinodular, contrast-enhancing pattern consistent with a granulomatous disease (eg, infection by mycobacteria, fungi, parasite, or even sarcoidosis).2,3 The differential diagnosis is narrowed largely by the CSF characteristics. Eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is defined as the presence of more than 10 eosinophils/mm3in CSF and/or eosinophils accounting for more than 10% of cerebrospinal leukocytes.4The most common cause of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is invasion of the central nervous system by helminthic parasites, such asAngiostrongylus cantonensis, Gnathostomaspecies, Schistosoma mansoni,andTaenia solium.5Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis may present eosinophilia and neuromyelitis-optica spectrum disorders may present some eosinophils in the CSF, but we would not expect sufficient eosinophils to fulfill the definition of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis in these diseases. With the history of recent travel to northeastern Brazil, an endemic region forS mansoni, we ordered immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin M antibody tests for this parasite in the patient’s CSF, of which results were positive. We also tested for antibodies in the blood using the enzyme-linked immunoassay  method, of which results were undetermined. Different from antibodies in the CSF, antibody detection in blood samples cannot distinguish between prior and active infection and have limited specificity for the diagnosis of neuroschistomiasis in endemic areas.6 Results for Kato-Katz testing forS mansonieggs were negative. However, this test has low sensitivity, especially when a single sample is used because egg burden in feces may be uneven and may lack sensitivity in the acute phase of infection because it may take up to 2 months for the adult worms to deposit the eggs in the bowel wall.7 We believe the present patient fulfills the diagnosis of neuroschistosomiasis according to criteria proposed by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention8: (1) typical syndrome as eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is suggestive of an infection caused by helminths, including schistosomiasis, (2) evidence of schistosomiasis demonstrated by the presence of positive immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G  antibodies forS mansoniin the CSF, and (3) a reasonable exclusion of the differential diagnosis. Neuroschistosomiasis can develop during any stage of the infection byS mansoni.However, an intense granulomatous response with clinically significant eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, eosinophilia, patchy pulmonary infiltrates, the presence of immunoglobulin M antibodies in the CSF, the absence of eggs in the Kato-Katz testing, and the presumed exposure are all suggestive of the acute phase of the infection that usually occurs 28 to 90 days after the infection and precedes oviposition.6 In Brazil, the most common presentation of neuroschistosomiasis is myeloradiculopathy owing to the parasite migration via the Batson venous plexus. However, case reports and a systematic review of 33 cases published from 1989 to 2019 of cerebral infection withS mansonishowed that brainstem lesions can also occur.9 There is a concern for initial worsening of neurologic symptoms with administration of anthelmintic therapy with praziquantel because the egg destruction may lead to further central nervous system inflammation. Although there is a lack of consensus on the optimal treatment of neuroschistosomiasis, many authors believe this complication can be prevented by corticosteroids, usually prednisone 1 to 2 mg/kg/d, started a few days before the initiation of praziquantel and continued for at least 2 months.10 Even with adequate therapy for neuroschistosomiasis, this patient presented with severe dysphagia and was submitted to orotracheal intubation. Unfortunately, she developed ventilator-associated complications and died.

case_info.explanation: Although listeriosis is a major cause of rhombencephalitis, the CSF typically does not show eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, and the patient’s blood and CSF cultures were sterile. Beyond listeriosis, other infections (herpesvirus infections and tuberculosis) and autoimmune diseases (Behçet disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis, demyelinating diseases, and paraneoplastic syndromes) may cause rhombencephalitis.1The patient presented with a nodular lesion with an heterogenous, multinodular, contrast-enhancing pattern consistent with a granulomatous disease (eg, infection by mycobacteria, fungi, parasite, or even sarcoidosis).2,3 The differential diagnosis is narrowed largely by the CSF characteristics. Eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is defined as the presence of more than 10 eosinophils/mm3in CSF and/or eosinophils accounting for more than 10% of cerebrospinal leukocytes.4The most common cause of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is invasion of the central nervous system by helminthic parasites, such asAngiostrongylus cantonensis, Gnathostomaspecies, Schistosoma mansoni,andTaenia solium.5Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis may present eosinophilia and neuromyelitis-optica spectrum disorders may present some eosinophils in the CSF, but we would not expect sufficient eosinophils to fulfill the definition of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis in these diseases. With the history of recent travel to northeastern Brazil, an endemic region forS mansoni, we ordered immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin M antibody tests for this parasite in the patient’s CSF, of which results were positive. We also tested for antibodies in the blood using the enzyme-linked immunoassay  method, of which results were undetermined. Different from antibodies in the CSF, antibody detection in blood samples cannot distinguish between prior and active infection and have limited specificity for the diagnosis of neuroschistomiasis in endemic areas.6 Results for Kato-Katz testing forS mansonieggs were negative. However, this test has low sensitivity, especially when a single sample is used because egg burden in feces may be uneven and may lack sensitivity in the acute phase of infection because it may take up to 2 months for the adult worms to deposit the eggs in the bowel wall.7 We believe the present patient fulfills the diagnosis of neuroschistosomiasis according to criteria proposed by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention8: (1) typical syndrome as eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is suggestive of an infection caused by helminths, including schistosomiasis, (2) evidence of schistosomiasis demonstrated by the presence of positive immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G  antibodies forS mansoniin the CSF, and (3) a reasonable exclusion of the differential diagnosis. Neuroschistosomiasis can develop during any stage of the infection byS mansoni.However, an intense granulomatous response with clinically significant eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, eosinophilia, patchy pulmonary infiltrates, the presence of immunoglobulin M antibodies in the CSF, the absence of eggs in the Kato-Katz testing, and the presumed exposure are all suggestive of the acute phase of the infection that usually occurs 28 to 90 days after the infection and precedes oviposition.6 In Brazil, the most common presentation of neuroschistosomiasis is myeloradiculopathy owing to the parasite migration via the Batson venous plexus. However, case reports and a systematic review of 33 cases published from 1989 to 2019 of cerebral infection withS mansonishowed that brainstem lesions can also occur.9 There is a concern for initial worsening of neurologic symptoms with administration of anthelmintic therapy with praziquantel because the egg destruction may lead to further central nervous system inflammation. Although there is a lack of consensus on the optimal treatment of neuroschistosomiasis, many authors believe this complication can be prevented by corticosteroids, usually prednisone 1 to 2 mg/kg/d, started a few days before the initiation of praziquantel and continued for at least 2 months.10 Even with adequate therapy for neuroschistosomiasis, this patient presented with severe dysphagia and was submitted to orotracheal intubation. Unfortunately, she developed ventilator-associated complications and died.
